issues.legal_issue: Recognition of an inam grant requires an express acknowledgment by the government or an unequivocal act acknowledging the grantee’s title; mere inaction is insufficient unless the surrounding circumstances compel the conclusion that the government acknowledged the title.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether inam villages qualified as estates because their grants had been recognised by the British Government.
The government had sometimes investigated inam titles and issued title deeds, while other grants had not been investigated or expressly recognised.
The government’s Inam Rules provided a procedure for investigating titles but did not themselves determine or acknowledge any particular grantee’s title.
issues.conclusion: For the purposes of section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, recognition means an express acknowledgment of the grantee’s title or an acknowledgment by an unequivocal government act. Acquiescence may amount to recognition only where the circumstances inevitably lead to that conclusion; mere inaction does not. The Inam Rules alone do not confer or recognise title.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, recognition requires an acknowledgment by the government, expressly or by an unequivocal act. Acquiescence can suffice only when compelling surrounding circumstances make recognition inevitable; mere inaction does not. The Court approved Secretary of State for India v. Bhavamurthy (1912) and Sam v. Ramalinga Mudaliar (1916), and disapproved observations in Mantravadi Bhavanarayana v. Merugu Venkatadu (1954) and P. V. Narayana Rao v. State of Orissa (1956) suggesting that mere inaction constitutes recognition. The Inam Rules of 1859 prescribed a procedure for investigating titles and did not themselves confer or recognise title.

issues.definition: A grant is recognised when, in an estate-classification case, the government expressly or unequivocally acknowledges its title, or when compelling circumstances make that acknowledgment inevitable.

issues.legal_issue: A government decision to discontinue action after an inquiry into competing claims to inam villages can amount to recognition of the inamdars’ title where the decision accepts that they hold under the zamindar.
material_facts: The government investigated pre-settlement inams and gave notice that the villages might be enfranchised.
The zamindar objected, claiming that the villages formed part of the zamindari and that the government had no reversionary right in them.
After reconsidering the matter, the government decided to take no further action concerning settlement of the inams.
The government’s decision in those circumstances accepted the claim that the inamdars held the villages under the zamindar.
issues.conclusion: The government’s decision to take no further action amounted to recognition of the inamdars’ titles. The villages therefore fell within the relevant statutory definition of an estate, and the appeals concerning them were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, recognition may be inferred from conduct where the surrounding circumstances compel that conclusion. Here, an inquiry, competing claims by the government and the zamindar, and the government’s withdrawal of further action showed acknowledgment of the inamdars’ title to hold under the zamindar.

issues.legal_issue: Mere inaction where no inquiry or other government act acknowledging title is shown does not establish recognition, and the government’s general rules for investigating inams do not themselves recognise particular grants.
material_facts: For a group of the villages, the record showed no government-directed inquiry into the inam titles and no other government act acknowledging those titles.
The High Court treated the government’s inaction as recognition.
The government relied on its Inam Rules, which provided for title inquiries and confirmation based on possession, but no relevant inquiry had been held for those villages.
The High Court had not determined disputed factual questions bearing on whether the villages qualified as estates on other grounds.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in treating mere inaction as recognition, and the Inam Rules did not establish recognition of the grants. The judgment was set aside and the affected appeals were remanded for determination of the remaining disputed questions.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, requires an acknowledgment of title by an express or unequivocal government act, or circumstances making that acknowledgment inevitable. The Inam Rules of 1859 provided only a procedure for ascertaining titles and did not proprio vigore confer or recognise any inamdar’s title. Because the High Court had not decided disputed factual issues, the affected appeals were remanded.

issues.legal_issue: An alternative statutory ground that depends on proof of facts and is raised for the first time on appeal need not be considered.
material_facts: The State argued for the first time before the Supreme Court that villages not covered by the definition in the Madras Estates Land Act could nevertheless qualify as estates under the Orissa Estates Abolition Act.
The alternative argument depended on proof of the conditions specified in that Act.
The argument raised a mixed question of fact and law, and the State had not raised it in the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the alternative contention because it was raised for the first time and depended on proof of facts; it expressed no opinion on the contention’s merits.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain a new contention involving a mixed question of fact and law where its determination depended on proof of statutory conditions and it had not been raised in the High Court. The contention invoked section 2(g) of the Orissa Estates Abolition Act, 1952; the Court left its merits open.
